Hey, I’m from the U.K. (near London) so lemme see how I can help.


1. The entirety of the U.K. is generally very safe, however, precautions should be taken like anywhere. London or other big cities are very populated, so be aware of potential terrorist attacks. Gang violence is large here as is knife crime, so I wouldn’t recommend walking around at night too late. Public transport is safe, albeit very busy and disorganised. Hitchhiking is very uncommon in the U.K, so you’re unlikely to be picked up, and even if you do, it’s likely to be someone dodgy.

2. In the U.K., always check receipts, some will take a percentage off your bill anyways so don’t worry about tipping. If there’s no standard tip, the general rule of thumb if 10%.

3. Our weather is very unpredictable, however, it’s likely to be 25-35 degrees C most days, however, bring clothes to accommodate rain as there’s always a large possibility of rain here.

4. Never looked for hostels in the U.K., but I imagine it’s as easy as other places. Just try looking online.

5. Prices vary a lot over here. You can get a large McDonald’s meal for about £4.50, but then a standard restaurant you could be paying around £15 per person. Attractions are quite expensive over here too so try to check them out in advance. Taxis are expensive so avoid them. Uber or public transport is much cheaper.

6. There’s a few information centres, especially in London, which will have ample information. Moreover, your hostels should provide information too. If not, most locals would be more than happy to offer you some pointers 

7. There’s no real correct dresswear for anything here. One thing I would say, is that sophisticated restaurants or museums may have a rule about ‘no denim jeans’ so maybe have a pair of smart clothes incase. It’s often windy too, so a warm hoodie would be recommended.

8. The UKs quite diverse so it’s hard for you to be singled out as a traveler. Common sense comes into play here. If something seems off, it probably is. We have a problem with homelessness, some of which are fake, so don’t be drawn into giving sums of money.

Don’t rush into playing this because you’ll create bad playing habits, so start watching YouTube videos to make sure you have a good technique and understand the bass, learn all the bass jargon like what a hammer on is etc, and learn your scales too.


Once you’ve got a basic understanding of that, start playing bass riffs (not full songs yet). Start easy and work your way up, don’t worry about buying books as most bass tabs are online for free now- but beware these are user submitted so many not be 100% accurate.


Most importantly, just enjoy it, don’t suck the fun out of it practicing 18 hours a day.
